Lemma 6.4.

Let SS be a Bézout domain which is contained in a field LL, and P∈Matm,n⁡(S)P\in\operatorname{Mat}_{m,n}(S). If r≥rk⁡P>0r\geq\operatorname{rk}P>0, then there exists a Q∈Matm,r⁡(S)Q\in\operatorname{Mat}_{m,r}(S) which is left invertible over SS, such that P=Q​AP=QA for some A∈Matr,n⁡(S)A\in\operatorname{Mat}_{r,n}(S).

Proof.

Just like in the algorithm to compute the Smith normal form of a matrix over a principal ideal domain, we can multiply PP with an invertible matrix from the left, to obtain a matrix of which the first nonzero column is zero below the first row. If we recurse this on the submatrix without the first row, we see that we can multiply PP with an invertible matrix Q~\tilde{Q} from the left, to obtain a matrix A~\tilde{A} in row-echelon form. All nonzero entries of A~\tilde{A} are within the submatrix of the first rr rows of A~\tilde{A}, which we call AA. For QQ, we take the submatrix of the first rr columns of Q~\tilde{Q}. ∎

Corollary 6.5.

Let S=K⁡[t]S=K[t], L=K⁡(t)L=K(t) and P∈Matm,n⁡(S)P\in\operatorname{Mat}_{m,n}(S). If r≥rk⁡P>0r\geq\operatorname{rk}P>0, then there exists matrices QQ and AA as in lemma 6.4, such that in addition, the leading homogeneous parts of the columns of QQ are independent over LL. In other words, the matrix Q^∈Matm,n⁡(K)\hat{Q}\in\operatorname{Mat}_{m,n}(K), which is defined by that Q^​ei\hat{Q}e_{i} is the column of the coefficients of tdeg⁡(Q​ei)t^{\deg(Qe_{i})} of QiQ_{i}, has rank rr.

Proof.

Since K⁡[t]K[t] is a Bézout domain, we can find matrices QQ and AA as in lemma 6.4. Assume without loss of generality that

deg⁡(Q​e1)≤deg⁡(Q​e2)≤⋯≤deg⁡(Q​er)\deg(Qe_{1})\leq\deg(Qe_{2})\leq\cdots\leq\deg(Qe_{r})

Suppose that the leading homogeneous parts of the columns of QQ are dependent over LL. Then there exists an ii such that Q^​ei\hat{Q}e_{i} is dependent over KK on Q^​e1,Q^​e2,…,Q^​ei−1\hat{Q}e_{1},\hat{Q}e_{2},\ldots,\hat{Q}e_{i-1}, say that Q^​ei=c1​Q^​e1+c2​Q^​e2+⋯+ci−1​Q^​ei−1\hat{Q}e_{i}=c_{1}\hat{Q}e_{1}+c_{2}\hat{Q}e_{2}+\cdots+c_{i-1}\hat{Q}e_{i-1}.

Now replace QQ by

Q−∑j=1i−1cj​tdeg⁡(Q​ei)−deg⁡(Q​ej)​Q^​ejQ-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}c_{j}t^{\deg(Qe_{i})-\deg(Qe_{j})}\hat{Q}e_{j}

Then QQ is replaced by Q​UQU for an upper diagonal U∈Matr⁡(S)U\in\operatorname{Mat}_{r}(S) with ones on the diagonal. So U∈GLr⁡(S)U\in\operatorname{GL}_{r}(S) and we can replace AA by U−1​AU^{-1}A to preserve P=Q​AP=QA. Similarly, it follows that QQ remains left invertible over SS.

By induction on deg⁡Q​e1+deg⁡Q​e2+⋯+deg⁡Q​er\deg Qe_{1}+\deg Qe_{2}+\cdots+\deg Qe_{r}, it follows that we can get AA and QQ as claimed after repeating the above several times. ∎

One can apply lemma 6.4 another time on the transpose of the matrix AA from the first application, to obtain that AA is the product of a triangular matrix BB of size r×rr\times r and a right-invertible matrix. This yields a weak version of a result from 1861 by Henri John Stephen Smith in [Smi]. The result of Smith is essentially that BB is even a diagonal matrix, such that the diagonal entries of BB are ordered by divisibility. The Smith normal form of matrix PP is just the diagonal matrix BB, filled up with zero entries on the right and below so it has the same dimensions as PP.

But Smith assumed the ring SS to be noetherian, i.e. a principal ideal domain. However, there exist Bézout domains for which Smith’s result is valid, and no Bézout domains are known for which Smith’s result is not valid, see [Kap].

7 Hessians with small rank over polynomial rings

In (iii) of theorem 6.2, RR is assumed to be a Bézout domain, so RR cannot be a multivariate polynomial ring over a field. But we will allow RR to be any polynomial ring over a field of characteristic zero in our main theorem. To cover the case of RR being a polynomial ring in (v) of theorem 7.2 below, we make the following definition.

Definition 7.1.

Let KK be a field and RR be an integral KK-domain. Let LL be the fraction field of RR. We call RR Bogal if one of the following statements is satisfied.

  • •

    RR is a Bézout domain.

  • •

    RR is a gcd\gcd-domain and LL satisfies Lüroth’s theorem as an extension field of KK.

Here, Bogal stands for ‘Bézout or gcd\gcd and Lüroth’.

Theorem 7.2 (Main theorem).

    where g∈Rg\in R and b∈Rm∖Kmb\in R^{m}\setminus K^{m}. Furthermore, H=bH=b.

    Suppose that trdegK⁡K⁡(H)=2\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)=2 and that HH does have an image apex a∈Kma\in K^{m} over KK. If RR is a gcd\gcd-domain, then hh is of the form

    h=g⁡(p1​x1+p2​x2+⋯+pm​xm)+a1​x1+a2​x2+⋯+am​xmh=g(p_{1}x_{1}+p_{2}x_{2}+\cdots+p_{m}x_{m})+a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}+\cdots+a_{m}x_{m}

    where g∈R⁡[t]g\in R[t] and p,b∈Rmp,b\in R^{m}, such that deg⁡b≥1\deg b\geq 1. In addition,

Suppose that R⁡[x]R[x] is graded with a torsion-free group, such that KK has trivial grading. If the components of HH are either zero or graded homogeneous of fixed degree, then a=0a=0 is an image apex of HH.

Corollary 7.3 (Main corollary).

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and h∈K⁡[x]h\in K[x]. Let r:=rk⁡ℋ​hr:=\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{H}}h and let ss be the number of independent projective image apices of ∇h\nabla h. Let m:=n−sm:=n-s and assume without loss of generality that em+1,em+2,…,ene_{m+1},e_{m+2},\ldots,e_{n} are ss independent projective image apices of ∇h\nabla h.

Define R:=K⁡[xm+1,xm+2,…,xn]R:=K[x_{m+1},x_{m+2},\ldots,x_{n}].

  1. (i)

    Suppose that ∇h\nabla h does not have an image apex.

    • •

      If r≤2r\leq 2, then r=2r=2, hh is of the form of (ii) of theorem 7.2 and s=1s=1.

    • •

      If r=3r=3 and s≥1s\geq 1, then hh is of the form of (ii) or (iv) of theorem 7.2 and s=2s=2 or s=1s=1 respectively.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose that ∇h\nabla h does have an image apex.

    • •

      If r≤2r\leq 2, then hh is of the form of (i) of theorem 7.2 and s=rs=r.

    • •

      If r=3r=3, then hh is of the form of (i) or (iii) of theorem 7.2 and s=3s=3 or s=1s=1 respectively.

    • •

      If r=4r=4 and s≥1s\geq 1, then hh is of the form of (i), (iii) or (v) of theorem 7.2 and s=4s=4, s=2s=2 or s=1s=1 respectively.

  3. (iii)

    Suppose that hh is homogeneous. If r≥1r\geq 1, then the zero vector is an image apex of ∇h\nabla h.

    • •

      If 1≤r≤31\leq r\leq 3, then hh is of the form of (i) of theorem 7.2 with ai=0a_{i}=0 for all ii and s=rs=r.

    • •

      If r=4r=4, then hh is of the form of (i) or (iii) of theorem 7.2 with ai=0a_{i}=0 for all ii and s=4s=4 or s=2s=2 respectively.

Proof.

Notice that RR is both a gcd\gcd-domain and a Bogal domain (but not necessarily a Bézout domain). Let H=(∂∂x1​h,∂∂x2​h,…,∂∂xm​h)H=\big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}h,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}h,\ldots,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}h\big). From proposition 1.2.9 of either [vdE], it follows that r=trdegK⁡K⁡(∇h)r=\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(\nabla h).

From (ii) of proposition 3.9, it follows that HH does not have a projective image apex p∈Kmp\in K^{m} over KK. From (i) of proposition 3.9, it follows that ∇h\nabla{h} has an image apex a∈Kna\in K^{n} over KK, if and only if HH has an image apex a∈Kma\in K^{m} over KK. From (iii) of proposition 3.9, it follows that trdegK⁡K⁡(H)=r−s\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)=r-s. Hence the results follow from lemma 6.1 and theorem 7.2 ∎

Proof of (i) of theorem 7.2.

As trdegK⁡K⁡(H)=0\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)=0 and KK is algebraically closed in LL, it follows that H∈KmH\in K^{m}. So if we take a:=Ha:=H, then it is straightforward to verify that (i) is satisfied. ∎

Proof of (ii) of theorem 7.2.

Notice that

0≤trdegL⁡L⁡(H)≤trdegK⁡K⁡(H)=10\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)=1

We first show that trdegL⁡L⁡(H)=0\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)=0. So assume that trdegL⁡L⁡(H)=1\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)=1. On account of (i) and (ii) of lemma 6.1, HH has a projective image apex p∈Lmp\in L^{m} over LL, in particular over KK. From (i) of theorem 4.9, it follows that trdegL⁡L⁡(H)≤trdegK⁡K⁡(H)−1=0\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)-1=0, so trdegL⁡L⁡(H)=0\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)=0.

On account of (i) of theorem 6.2, hh is of the form

h=g+b1​x1+b2​x2+⋯+bm​xmh=g+b_{1}x_{1}+b_{2}x_{2}+\cdots+b_{m}x_{m}

where g∈Rg\in R and b∈Rmb\in R^{m} is any image apex of HH over LL which is contained in RmR^{m}. Since trdegK⁡K⁡(H)=1\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)=1, it follows that b=H∉Kmb=H\notin K^{m}.

So it remains to show the first claim of (ii). Hence suppose that HH does have an image apex a∈Kma\in K^{m} over KK. Since trdegL⁡L⁡(H)>−1=trdegK⁡K⁡(H)−2\operatorname{trdeg}_{L}L(H)>-1=\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}K(H)-2, it follows from (iii) of theorem 4.9 that aa is an image apex of HH over LL. Hence we can take b=ab=a. This contradicts b=H∉Kmb=H\notin K^{m}, so HH does not have an image apex a∈Kma\in K^{m} over KK. ∎

Lemma 7.6 (Lefschetz’s principle for torsion-free group gradings).

Suppose that RR is a commutative ring which is graded with a torsion-free group, such that KK has trivial grading. Let GG be the grading subgroup of RR, i.e. all group elements which are generated by the degrees of graded homogeneous components of elements of RR.

Let R~\tilde{R} be the subring of RR which is generated by the graded homogeneous components of elements c1,c2,c3,…∈Rc_{1},c_{2},c_{3},\ldots\in R, and G~\tilde{G} be the grading subgroup of R~\tilde{R}. Then there exists a homomorphism from GG to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} which is injective on G~\tilde{G}.

Proof.

Since RR is commutative, we deduce that GG is a torsion-free abelian group. Hence GG is a torsion-free ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module. Since GG is torsion-free, we infer that GG embeds in its localization with respect to ℤ∖{0}{\mathbb{Z}}\setminus\{0\}. This localization is a vector space VV over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Assume without loss of generality that G⊆VG\subseteq V. Notice that G~\tilde{G} is at most countably generated, say by 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}. On account of Zermelo’s well-ordering theorem, there exists a well-ordering on both 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} and V∖𝒞V\setminus{\mathcal{C}}, which we combine to a well-ordering of VV by assuming that elements of 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} are smaller than those of V∖𝒞V\setminus{\mathcal{C}}.

Let ℬ{\mathcal{B}} be the subset of nonzero elements of VV which cannot be written as a linear combination of smaller elements of VV. Then the elements of ℬ{\mathcal{B}} are linearly independent, because the largest element of ℬ{\mathcal{B}} in a possible dependence relation does not exist. We show that every nonzero element v∈V∖ℬv\in V\setminus{\mathcal{B}} is a linear combination of elements of ℬ{\mathcal{B}} which are smaller than vv. Suppose that this is not the case, and let vv be the smallest counterexample. Since v∉ℬv\notin{\mathcal{B}}, we can write vv as a linear combination of smaller elements ww of VV. Each of these ww is either contained in ℬ{\mathcal{B}}, or a linear combination of elements of ℬ{\mathcal{B}} which are smaller than ww and hence also smaller than vv. Contradiction.

Let 𝒟=𝒞∩ℬ{\mathcal{D}}={\mathcal{C}}\cap{\mathcal{B}}. Then 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} is a basis of the linear span of 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}, which extends to a basis ℬ{\mathcal{B}} of VV. Since 𝒟⊆𝒞{\mathcal{D}}\subseteq{\mathcal{C}}, we see that 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} is at most countable, say 𝒟={d1,d2,d3,…}{\mathcal{D}}=\{d_{1},d_{2},d_{3},\ldots\}. Now define a group homomorphism to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} by sending djd_{j} to ej{\mathrm{e}}^{j} for each j∈{1,2,3,…}j\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}, and sending elements of ℬ∖𝒟{\mathcal{B}}\setminus{\mathcal{D}} to 00, where e{\mathrm{e}} is Eulers number. Since e{\mathrm{e}} is transcendental over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, we deduce that G~\tilde{G} is embedded in ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. ∎
